sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen10853" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="28" osisID="Ps.28" sID="Ps.28"/> <div eID="gen10853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10854" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10855" type="x-p"/> The former part of this psalm is the prayer of a saint militan and now in distress (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.1-Ps.28.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), to which is added the doom of God's implacable enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.4-Ps.28.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. The latter part of the psalm is the thanksgiving of a saint triumphant, and delivered out of his distresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6-Ps.28.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), to which is added a prophetical prayer for all God's faithful loyal subjects, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">ver. 9</reference>. So that it is hard to say which of these two conditions David was in when he penned it. Some think he was now in trouble seeking God, but at the same time preparing to praise him for his deliverance, and by faith giving him thanks for it, before it was wrought. Others think he was now in triumph, but remembered, and recorded for his own and others' benefit, the prayers he made when he was in affliction, that the mercy might relish the better, when it appeared to be an answer to them.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10855" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10854" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for Deliverance.</title> <div sID="gen10856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Unto thee will I cry, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my rock; be not silent to me: lest, <hi type="italic">if</hi> thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle. 3 Draw me not away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, which speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their hearts. <hi type="super">4</hi> Give them according to their deeds, and according to the wickedness of their endeavours: give them after the work of their hands; render to them their desert. 5 Because they regard not the works of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , nor the operation of his hands, he shall destroy them, and not build them up. <div eID="gen10856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10857" type="x-p"/> In these verses David is very earnest in prayer. <div eID="gen10857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> I. He prays that God would graciously hear and answer him, now that, in his distress, he called upon him, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1-Ps.28.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Observe his faith in prayer: <hi type="italic">O Lord, my rock,</hi> denoting his belief of God's power (he is a rock) and his dependence upon that power—"He is <hi type="italic">my rock,</hi> on whom I build my hope." Observe his fervency in prayer: "<hi type="italic">To thee will I cry,</hi> as one in earnest, being ready to sink, unless thou come in with seasonable succour." And observe how solicitous he is to obtain an answer: <hi type="italic">"Be not silent to me,</hi> as one angry at my prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">Ps. lxxx. 4</reference>. Lord, speak to me, answer me <hi type="italic">with good words and comfortable words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zech. i. 13</reference>); though the thing I pray for has not been given me, yet let God speak to me joy and gladness, and make me to hear them. Lord, speak for me, in answer to my prayers, plead my cause, command deliverances for me, and thus hear and answer the voice of my supplications." Two things he pleads:—1. The sad despair he should be in if God slighted him: "<hi type="italic">If thou be silent to me,</hi> and I have not the tokens of thy favour, I am <hi type="italic">like those that go down into the pit</hi> (that is, I am a dead man, lost and undone); if God be not my friend, appear not to me and appear not for me, my hope and my help will have perished." Nothing can be so cutting, so killing, to a gracious soul, as the want of God's favour and the sense of his displeasure. <hi type="italic">I shall be like those that go down to hell</hi> (so some understand it); for what is the misery of the damned but this, that God is ever silent to them and deaf to their cry? Those are in some measure qualified for God's favour, and may expect it, who are thus possessed with a dread of his wrath, and to whom his frowns are worse than death. 2. The good hopes he had that God would favour him: <hi type="italic">I lift up my hands towards thy holy oracle,</hi> which denotes, not only an earnest desire, but an earnest expectation, thence to receive an answer of peace. The most holy place within the veil is here, as elsewhere, called the <hi type="italic">oracle;</hi> there the ark and the mercy-seat were, there God was said to <hi type="italic">dwell between the cherubim,</hi> and thence he spoke to his people, <reference osisRef="Num.7.89">Num. vii. 89</reference>. That was a type of Christ, and it is to him that we must lift up our eyes and hands, for through him all good comes from God to us. It was also a figure of heaven (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">Heb. ix. 24</reference>); and from God as our Father in heaven we are taught to expect an answer to our prayers. The scriptures are called <hi type="italic">the oracles of God,</hi> and to them we must have an eye in our prayers and expectations. There is the word on which God hath caused and encouraged us to hope. <div eID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> II. He deprecates the doom of wicked people, as before (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Ps. xxvi. 9</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Gather not my soul with sinners</hi>): Lord, I attend thy holy oracle, <hi type="italic">draw me not away</hi> from that <hi type="italic">with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">v. 3</reference>. 1. "Save me from being entangled in the snares they have laid for me. They flatter and cajole me, and speak peace to me; but they have a design upon me, for <hi type="italic">mischief is in their heart;</hi> they aim to disturb me, nay, to destroy me. Lord, suffer me not to be drawn away and ruined by their cursed plots; for they have, can have, no power, no success, against me, except it be given them from above." 2. "Save me from being infected with their sins and from doing as they do. Let me not be drawn away by their fallacious arguments, or their allurements, from the holy oracle (where I desire to dwell all the days of my life), to practise any wicked works;" see <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Ps. cxli. 4</reference>. "Lord, never leave me to myself, to use such arts of deceit and treachery for my safety as they use to my ruin. Let no event of Providence be an invincible temptation to me, to draw me either into the imitation or into the interest of wicked people." Good men dread the way of sinners; the best are sensible of the danger they are in of being drawn aside into it; and therefore we should all pray earnestly to God for his grace to keep us in our integrity. 3. "Save me from being involved in their doom; let me not be led forth with the workers of iniquity, for I am not one of those that speak peace while war is in their hearts." Note, Those that are careful not to partake with sinners in their sins have reason to hope that they shall not partake with them in their plagues, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> III. He imprecates the just judgments of God upon the workers of iniquity (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give them according to their deeds.</hi> This is not the language of passion or revenge, nor is it inconsistent with the duty of praying for our enemies. But, 1. Thus he would show how far he was from complying with the workers of iniquity, and with what good reason he had begged not to be drawn away with them, because he was convinced that they could not be made more miserable then to be dealt with according to their deeds. 2. Thus he would express his zeal for the honour of God's justice in the governing world. "Lord, they think all well that they do, and justify themselves in their wicked practices. Lord, <hi type="italic">give them after the work of their hands,</hi> and so undeceive those about them, who think there is no harm in what they do because it goes unpunished," <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.2">Ps. xciv. 1, 2</reference>. 3. This prayer is a prophecy that God will, sooner or later, render to all impenitent sinners according to their deserts. If what has been done amiss be not undone by repentance, there will certainly come a reckoning day, when God will render to every man who persists in his evil deeds according to them. It is a prophecy particularly of the destruction of destroyers: "<hi type="italic">They speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts;</hi> Lord, <hi type="italic">give them according to their deeds,</hi> let the spoilers be spoiled, and let those be treacherously dealt with who have thus dealt treacherously;" see <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Rev. xviii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">xiii. 10</reference>. Observe, He foretels that God will reward them, not only according to their deed, but <hi type="italic">according to the wickedness of their endeavours;</hi> for sinners shall be reckoned with, not only for the mischief they have done, but for the mischief they would have done, which they designed, and did what they could to effect. And, if God go by this rule in dealing with the wicked, surely he will do so in dealing with the righteous, and will reward them, not only for the good they have done, but for the good they have endeavoured to do, though they could not accomplish it. <div eID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> IV. He foretels their destruction for their contempt of God and his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because they regard not the works of the Lord and the operations of his hands,</hi> by which he manifests himself and speaks to the children of men, <hi type="italic">he will destroy them</hi> in this world and in the other, <hi type="italic">and not build them up.</hi>" Note, A stupid regardlessness of the works of God is the cause of their ruin. Why do men question the being or attributes of God, but because they do not duly regard his handiworks, which declare his glory, and in which the invisible things of him are clearly seen? Why do men forget God, and live without him, nay, affront God, and live in rebellion against him, but because they consider not the instances of that wrath of his which is revealed <hi type="italic">from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men?</hi> Why do the enemies of God's people hate and persecute them, and devise mischief against them, but because they regard not the works God has wrought for his church, by which he has made it appear how dear it is to him? See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa. v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> In singing this we must arm ourselves against all temptations to join with the workers of iniquity, and animate ourselves against all the troubles we may be threatened with by the workers of iniquity.

Lord, speak to me, answer me with good words and comfortable words ( Zech. i. 13 ); though the thing I pray for has not been given me, yet let God speak to me joy and gladness, and make me to hear them. Lord, speak for me, in answer to my prayers, plead my cause, command deliverances for me, and thus hear and answer the voice of my supplications." Two things he pleads:—1. The sad despair he should be in if God slighted him: "<hi type="italic">If thou be silent to me,</hi> and I have not the tokens of thy favour, I am <hi type="italic">like those that go down into the pit</hi> (that is, I am a dead man, lost and undone); if God be not my friend, appear not to me and appear not for me, my hope and my help will have perished." Nothing can be so cutting, so killing, to a gracious soul, as the want of God's favour and the sense of his displeasure. <hi type="italic">I shall be like those that go down to hell</hi> (so some understand it); for what is the misery of the damned but this, that God is ever silent to them and deaf to their cry? Those are in some measure qualified for God's favour, and may expect it, who are thus possessed with a dread of his wrath, and to whom his frowns are worse than death. 2. The good hopes he had that God would favour him: <hi type="italic">I lift up my hands towards thy holy oracle,</hi> which denotes, not only an earnest desire, but an earnest expectation, thence to receive an answer of peace. The most holy place within the veil is here, as elsewhere, called the <hi type="italic">oracle;</hi> there the ark and the mercy-seat were, there God was said to <hi type="italic">dwell between the cherubim,</hi> and thence he spoke to his people, <reference osisRef="Num.7.89">Num. vii. 89</reference>. That was a type of Christ, and it is to him that we must lift up our eyes and hands, for through him all good comes from God to us. It was also a figure of heaven (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">Heb. ix. 24</reference>); and from God as our Father in heaven we are taught to expect an answer to our prayers. The scriptures are called <hi type="italic">the oracles of God,</hi> and to them we must have an eye in our prayers and expectations. There is the word on which God hath caused and encouraged us to hope. <div eID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> II. He deprecates the doom of wicked people, as before (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Ps. xxvi. 9</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Gather not my soul with sinners</hi>): Lord, I attend thy holy oracle, <hi type="italic">draw me not away</hi> from that <hi type="italic">with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">v. 3</reference>. 1. "Save me from being entangled in the snares they have laid for me. They flatter and cajole me, and speak peace to me; but they have a design upon me, for <hi type="italic">mischief is in their heart;</hi> they aim to disturb me, nay, to destroy me. Lord, suffer me not to be drawn away and ruined by their cursed plots; for they have, can have, no power, no success, against me, except it be given them from above." 2. "Save me from being infected with their sins and from doing as they do. Let me not be drawn away by their fallacious arguments, or their allurements, from the holy oracle (where I desire to dwell all the days of my life), to practise any wicked works;" see <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Ps. cxli. 4</reference>. "Lord, never leave me to myself, to use such arts of deceit and treachery for my safety as they use to my ruin. Let no event of Providence be an invincible temptation to me, to draw me either into the imitation or into the interest of wicked people." Good men dread the way of sinners; the best are sensible of the danger they are in of being drawn aside into it; and therefore we should all pray earnestly to God for his grace to keep us in our integrity. 3. "Save me from being involved in their doom; let me not be led forth with the workers of iniquity, for I am not one of those that speak peace while war is in their hearts." Note, Those that are careful not to partake with sinners in their sins have reason to hope that they shall not partake with them in their plagues, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> III. He imprecates the just judgments of God upon the workers of iniquity (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give them according to their deeds.</hi> This is not the language of passion or revenge, nor is it inconsistent with the duty of praying for our enemies. But, 1. Thus he would show how far he was from complying with the workers of iniquity, and with what good reason he had begged not to be drawn away with them, because he was convinced that they could not be made more miserable then to be dealt with according to their deeds. 2. Thus he would express his zeal for the honour of God's justice in the governing world. "Lord, they think all well that they do, and justify themselves in their wicked practices. Lord, <hi type="italic">give them after the work of their hands,</hi> and so undeceive those about them, who think there is no harm in what they do because it goes unpunished," <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.2">Ps. xciv. 1, 2</reference>. 3. This prayer is a prophecy that God will, sooner or later, render to all impenitent sinners according to their deserts. If what has been done amiss be not undone by repentance, there will certainly come a reckoning day, when God will render to every man who persists in his evil deeds according to them. It is a prophecy particularly of the destruction of destroyers: "<hi type="italic">They speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts;</hi> Lord, <hi type="italic">give them according to their deeds,</hi> let the spoilers be spoiled, and let those be treacherously dealt with who have thus dealt treacherously;" see <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Rev. xviii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">xiii. 10</reference>. Observe, He foretels that God will reward them, not only according to their deed, but <hi type="italic">according to the wickedness of their endeavours;</hi> for sinners shall be reckoned with, not only for the mischief they have done, but for the mischief they would have done, which they designed, and did what they could to effect. And, if God go by this rule in dealing with the wicked, surely he will do so in dealing with the righteous, and will reward them, not only for the good they have done, but for the good they have endeavoured to do, though they could not accomplish it. <div eID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> IV. He foretels their destruction for their contempt of God and his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because they regard not the works of the Lord and the operations of his hands,</hi> by which he manifests himself and speaks to the children of men, <hi type="italic">he will destroy them</hi> in this world and in the other, <hi type="italic">and not build them up.</hi>" Note, A stupid regardlessness of the works of God is the cause of their ruin. Why do men question the being or attributes of God, but because they do not duly regard his handiworks, which declare his glory, and in which the invisible things of him are clearly seen? Why do men forget God, and live without him, nay, affront God, and live in rebellion against him, but because they consider not the instances of that wrath of his which is revealed <hi type="italic">from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men?</hi> Why do the enemies of God's people hate and persecute them, and devise mischief against them, but because they regard not the works God has wrought for his church, by which he has made it appear how dear it is to him? See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa. v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> In singing this we must arm ourselves against all temptations to join with the workers of iniquity, and animate ourselves against all the troubles we may be threatened with by the workers of iniquity.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Thanksgiving and Praise.</title> <div sID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because he hath heard the voice of my supplications. <hi type="super">7</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> their strength, and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the saving strength of his anointed. <hi type="super">9</hi> Save thy people, and bless thine inheritance: feed them also, and lift them up for ever. <div eID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10864" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen10864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10865" type="x-p"/> I. David gives God thanks for the audience of his prayers as affectionately as a few verses before he had begged it: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">v. 6</reference>. How soon are the saints' sorrows turned into songs and their prayers into praises! It was in faith that David prayed (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hear the voice of my supplications;</hi> and by the same faith he gives thanks (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">v. 6</reference>) that <hi type="italic">God has heard the voice of his supplications.</hi> Note, 1. Those that pray in faith may rejoice in hope. "He hath heard me (graciously accepted me) and I am as sure of a real answer as if I had it already." 2. What we win by prayer we must wear by praise. Has God heard our supplications? Let us then bless his name. <div eID="gen10865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10866" type="x-p"/> II. He encourages himself to hope in God for the perfecting of every thing that concerned him. Having given to God the glory of his grace (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">v. 6</reference>), he is humbly bold to take the comfort of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.7">v. 7</reference>. This is the method of attaining peace: let us begin with praise that is attainable. Let us first bless God and then bless ourselves. Observe, 1. His dependence upon God: "<hi type="italic">The Lord is my strength,</hi> to support me, and carry me on, through all my services and sufferings. He is <hi type="italic">my shield,</hi> to protect me from all the malicious designs of my enemies against me. I have chosen him to be so, I have always found him so, and I expect he will still be so." 2. His experience of the benefits of that dependence: "<hi type="italic">My heart trusted in him,</hi> and in his power and promise; and it has not been in vain to do so, for <hi type="italic">I am helped,</hi> I have been often helped; not only God has given to me, in his due time, the help I trusted to him for, but my very trusting in him has helped me, in the mean time, and kept me from fainting." <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Ps. xxvii. 13</reference>. The very actings of faith are present aids to a dropping spirit, and often help it at a dead lift. 3. His improvement of this experience. (1.) He had the pleasure of it: <hi type="italic">Therefore my heart greatly rejoices.</hi> The joy of a believer is seated in the heart, while, in the laughter of the fool, the heart is sorrowful. It is great joy, <hi type="italic">joy unspeakable and full of glory.</hi> The heart that truly believes shall in due time greatly rejoice; it is <hi type="italic">joy and peace in believing</hi> that we are to expect. (2.) God shall have the praise of it: when <hi type="italic">my heart greatly rejoices, with my song will I praise him.</hi> This must we express our gratitude; it is the least we can do; and others will hereby be invited and encouraged to trust in him too. <div eID="gen10866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10867" type="x-p"/> III. He pleases himself with the interest which all good people, through Christ, have in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord is their strength;</hi> not mine only, but the strength of every believer." Note, The saints rejoice in their friends' comforts as well as their own; for, as we have not the less benefit from the light of the sun, so neither from the light of Gods' countenance, for others' sharing therein; for we are sure there is enough for all and enough for each. This is our communion with all saints, that God is their strength and ours, Christ their Lord and ours, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1 Cor. i. 2</reference>. He is their strength, the strength of all Israel, because he is <hi type="italic">the saving strength of his anointed,</hi> that is, 1. Of David in the type. God, in strengthening him that was their king and fought their battles, strengthened the whole kingdom. He calls himself God's <hi type="italic">anointed</hi> because it was the unction he had received that exposed him to the envy of his enemies, and therefore entitled him to the divine protection. 2. Of Christ, his anointed, his Messiah, in the anti-type. God was his saving strength, qualified him for his undertaking and carried him through it; see <reference osisRef="Ps.89.21 Isa.49.5 Isa.50.7 Isa.50.9">Ps. lxxxix. 21; Isa. xlix. 5; l. 7, 9</reference>. And so he becomes their strength, the strength of all the saints; he strengthened him that is the church's head, and from him diffuses strength to all the members, has commanded his strength, and so <hi type="italic">strengthens what he has wrought for us;</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28 Ps.68.80 Ps.68.17 Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 28; lxxx. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen10867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10868" type="x-p"/> IV. He concludes with a short but comprehensive prayer for the church of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">v. 9</reference>. He prays for Israel, not as his people ("save my people, and bless my inheritance"), though they were so, but, "<hi type="italic">thine.</hi>" God's interest in them lay nearer his heart than his own. <hi type="italic">We are thy people</hi> is a good plea, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.9">Isa. lxiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">lxiii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">I am thine, save me.</hi> God's people are his inheritance, dear to him, and precious in his eyes; what little glory he has from this world he has from them. <hi type="italic">The Lord's portion is his people.</hi> That which he begs of God for them is, 1. That he would save them from their enemies and the dangers they were exposed to. 2. That he would bless them with all good, flowing from his favour, in performance of his promise, and amounting to a happiness for them. 3. That he would <hi type="italic">feed them,</hi> bless them with plenty, and especially the plenty of his ordinances, which are food to the soul. <hi type="italic">Rule them;</hi> so the margin. "Direct their counsels and actions aright, and overrule their affairs for good. Feed them, and rule them; sets pastors, set rulers, over them, that shall do their office with wisdom and understanding." 4. That he would <hi type="italic">lift them up for ever,</hi> lift them up out of their troubles and distresses, and do this, not only for those of that age, but for his people in every age to come, even to the end. "Lift them up into thy glorious kingdom, lift them up as high as heaven." There, and there only, will the saints be lifted up for ever, never more to sink or be depressed. Observe, Those, and those only, whom God feeds and rules, who are willing to be taught, and guided, and governed, by him, shall be saved, and blessed, and lifted up for ever.  <chapter eID="Ps.28"/> <div eID="gen10868" type="x-p"/>

Those that pray in faith may rejoice in hope. "He hath heard me (graciously accepted me) and I am as sure of a real answer as if I had it already." 2. What we win by prayer we must wear by praise. It is great joy, joy unspeakable and full of glory. The heart that truly believes shall in due time greatly rejoice; it is joy and peace in believing that we are to expect. (2.) He is their strength, the strength of all Israel, because he is the saving strength of his anointed, that is, 1. Of David in the type. God, in strengthening him that was their king and fought their battles, strengthened the whole kingdom. He calls himself God's anointed because it was the unction he had received that exposed him to the envy of his enemies, and therefore entitled him to the divine protection. 2. God's people are his inheritance, dear to him, and precious in his eyes; what little glory he has from this world he has from them. The Lord's portion is his people. "Direct their counsels and actions aright, and overrule their affairs for good. Feed them, and rule them; sets pastors, set rulers, over them, that shall do their office with wisdom and understanding." 4. navigation_sections.content_plain: The former part of this psalm is the prayer of a saint militan and now in distress ( ver. 1-3 ), to which is added the doom of God's implacable enemies, ver. 4, 5 . The latter part of the psalm is the thanksgiving of a saint triumphant, and delivered out of his distresses ( ver. 6-8 ), to which is added a prophetical prayer for all God's faithful loyal subjects, ver. 9 . So that it is hard to say which of these two conditions David was in when he penned it. Some think he was now in trouble seeking God, but at the same time preparing to praise him for his deliverance, and by faith giving him thanks for it, before it was wrought. Others think he was now in triumph, but remembered, and recorded for his own and others' benefit, the prayers he made when he was in affliction, that the mercy might relish the better, when it appeared to be an answer to them.

The latter part of the psalm is the thanksgiving of a saint triumphant, and delivered out of his distresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6-Ps.28.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), to which is added a prophetical prayer for all God's faithful loyal subjects, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">ver. 9</reference>. So that it is hard to say which of these two conditions David was in when he penned it. Some think he was now in trouble seeking God, but at the same time preparing to praise him for his deliverance, and by faith giving him thanks for it, before it was wrought. Others think he was now in triumph, but remembered, and recorded for his own and others' benefit, the prayers he made when he was in affliction, that the mercy might relish the better, when it appeared to be an answer to them.
